text: Austin Melvin Knight (December 16, 1854 – February 26, 1927) was an admiral in the United States Navy who served as commander in chief of the U.S. Asiatic Fleet from 1917 to 1918. Born in Ware, Massachusetts, to Charles Sanford Knight and Cordelia Cutter Knight, he was appointed to the U.S. Naval Academy from Florida on June 30, 1869, graduating in 1873. After serving as a passed midshipman, he was commissioned an ensign on July 16, 1874. He held various sea and shore assignments, including service on the ships Tuscarora, Constellation, Chicago, Monongahela, and Lancaster, and attended the Naval War College at Newport in 1901. He commanded the armed yacht Yankton off the Cuban coast from 1901 to 1903 and the gunboat Castine in the Atlantic from 1903 to 1904. From 1904 to 1907, he presided over a naval ordnance board and a joint Army-Navy board on smokeless powder, and was promoted to captain in 1907, receiving command of the armored cruiser Washington in the Pacific. He resumed leadership of the naval ordnance board in 1909. In November 1910, the monitor Puritan was wrecked by an explosion of four hundred pounds of gelatin during ordnance tests under Knight's direction; the board of inquiry found the monitor had sunk into mud despite remaining afloat for twenty-two hours, requiring a wrecking company to raise it. Congress blamed Knight for "culpable negligence and inefficiency in the performance of duty," and a court-martial of seven rear admirals convened at the Norfolk Navy Yard, honorably acquitting him. Secretary of the Navy George von Lengerke Meyer disapproved the finding and referred the case back, but the court reaffirmed the acquittal, and Knight was restored to active duty. During his detainment, his wife fell ill and died, and the court-martial threatened to derail his promotion to rear admiral, making him a sympathetic figure among fellow officers. Following his acquittal, Knight was promoted to rear admiral in May 1911 (backdated to January 29) and assigned to command the Narragansett Bay Naval Station. He served as commander in chief of the Atlantic Reserve Fleet from 1912 to 1913, interrupted by temporary duty commanding a special squadron of the armored cruisers Tennessee and Montana dispatched to the Eastern Mediterranean in November 1912 to protect American citizens in Turkey during the Balkan War. As President of the Naval War College from December 15, 1913, to February 16, 1917, Knight was extensively quoted in Hudson Maxim's 1915 book Defenseless America, which urged America to rearm. He aligned with naval reformers like Bradley Fiske and William Sims, advocating for a navy general staff headed by a chief of naval operations with authority over both the line and bureaus. President Woodrow Wilson and Secretary of the Navy Josephus Daniels opposed this idea, and Wilson instructed Daniels to reprimand Knight after he publicly supported a general staff in a speech in New York City. On May 22, 1917, Knight raised his flag aboard the armored cruiser Brooklyn as commander in chief of the Asiatic Fleet with the temporary rank of admiral, directing American naval operations during the Allied intervention at Vladivostok in the Russian Civil War and serving as chairman of a ten-nation council to preserve order in the Russian Far East. He relinquished command on December 7, 1918, and reverted to his permanent rank of rear admiral, transferring to the retired list on December 16, 1918. He was recalled to active duty from March 13, 1919, to June 30, 1920, to serve as Senior Member of the Board of Awards. Before the armistice, no medals had been awarded for World War I service, so on March 6, 1919, Secretary Daniels appointed Knight to head a board to review all recommendations for the Medal of Honor, Distinguished Service Medal, and Navy Cross, submitting a uniform list of recommended honors. The board included Knight and eight other retired officers, drawing harsh criticism because most had retired before the U.S. entered the war and none had experience in war zones (Knight himself had served in a distant theater). The Knight Board convened from March 17, 1919, to October 31, 1919, but was suddenly dissolved by Secretary Daniels before completing its work or receiving key recommendations. Daniels disregarded most of the board's recommendations and created his own list, which sparked outrage—particularly because every commanding officer of a ship sunk by the enemy received the Distinguished Service Medal, while many who sank enemy vessels received none. Many officers refused the medals, most notably Admiral William Sims. Daniels hastily reconvened the Knight Board, but the second session's recommendations were no better, as the final decision on medals remained solely with the Secretary of the Navy. This awards controversy directly led to the creation of a largely independent Navy Department Board of Decorations and Medals. Knight died on February 26, 1927, in Washington, D.C., and was buried at the Naval Academy Cemetery. He served as President of the Naval Historical Foundation from 1926 until his death. On November 17, 1930, he was posthumously advanced to admiral on the retired list with the date of rank February 26, 1927, in recognition of his World War I service. Knight was awarded the Distinguished Service Medal for meritorious service as commander in chief of the Asiatic Fleet during Allied operations at Vladivostok, Siberia, and received the Grand Cordon of the Rising Sun from the Japanese government. In 1901, he authored Modern Seamanship, a guide to shiphandling and safety that became known as the sailor's bible for both pleasure boaters and professional seamen, repeatedly updated for over eighty years, with its eighteenth edition published in 1988. Knight married Alice Tobey, step-daughter of Wisconsin Governor Harrison Ludington, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on January 3, 1878; Alice died the following year, shortly after giving birth to their daughter, also named Alice. In 1886, at Annapolis, Maryland, on April 29, he married Elizabeth Harwood Welsh. He and Elizabeth had three children: Dorothy, Richard, and Katharine, the latter of whom married Rear Admiral Forrest B. Royal during World War II. A younger sister, Bertha Knight Landes, served as mayor of Seattle, Washington, from 1926 to 1928, becoming the first female mayor of a major American city. Another younger sister, Jessie Knight Jordan, married David Starr Jordan, president of Stanford University. The destroyer USS Knight (DD-633), launched on September 27, 1941, was sponsored by his granddaughter, Elizabeth H. Royal, and was named in his honor.
